title: Understanding Program Structure
description: Learn the key components of a C# program.

data.text: Every C# program, no matter how simple or complex, follows a logical structure. Understanding these building blocks — namespaces, classes, methods, and statements — will help you read, write, and organize C# code effectively.

Think of a C# program as a set of nested containers. At the top level, namespaces organize your code into logical groups. Inside namespaces, classes act as blueprints for objects. Inside classes, methods define the behavior, and statements are the individual instructions that make up a method.

data.text: A `using` directive imports a namespace so you can use its types without fully qualifying their names. For example, `using System;` lets you write `Console.WriteLine()` instead of `System.Console.WriteLine()`.

data.title: Common Using Directives
items: `using System;` — Core types like Console, String, Math
`using static System.Console;` — Import static members directly (C# 6.0+)

data.title: Global Using Directives
data.text: In .NET 6+ projects, many common using directives are declared globally in a file like GlobalUsings.cs, so you don't need to repeat them in every file. This is configured in the project file with <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>.

A **namespace** is a container that groups related classes, structs, interfaces, and other types. Namespaces prevent naming conflicts and make it easier to organize large codebases. For example, `System.IO` contains file-related types, while `System.Net` contains networking types.

data.title: Using Namespaces for Organization
data.content: Organizing code with namespaces for models and services

data.title: Namespace Convention
data.text: A common convention is to use your company or project name as the root namespace, followed by feature areas. For example: `Contoso.Ecommerce.Models`, `Contoso.Ecommerce.Services`.

A **class** is a blueprint for creating objects. It defines the data (fields/properties) and behavior (methods) that objects of that type will have. Every C# program uses classes, even if you don't realize it — top-level statements are compiled into a class behind the scenes.

data.title: Class Members
items: **Properties** — Public accessors for fields with optional logic (e.g., `public string Name { get; set; }`)
**Methods** — Functions that define behavior (e.g., `public void Save() { ... }`)
**Constructors** — Special methods that run when creating a new instance (e.g., `public User(string name) { ... }`)
**Events** — Notifications that something has happened (e.g., `public event EventHandler? Saved;`)

data.text: Access modifiers control which parts of your code can see and use a class or its members. They are essential for encapsulation — hiding implementation details and exposing only what's necessary.

rows: Within the class and derived classes
Within the assembly OR derived classes

data.text: A **method** is a reusable block of code that performs a specific task. Methods are defined inside classes (or structs) and can be called from other parts of your program. Every method has a return type, a name, optional parameters, and a body containing statements.

data.title: Defining and Using Methods
data.content: A class with multiple methods showing different patterns

data.text: A **statement** is a complete instruction that performs an action, like declaring a variable, calling a method, or controlling flow with `if` or `for`. Statements typically end with a semicolon. An **expression** is a combination of values, variables, and operators that produces a single value, like `2 + 2` or `name.ToUpper()`.

terms.definition: A container that organizes related classes and types to prevent naming conflicts and improve code organization.
A blueprint or template that defines the data (fields/properties) and behavior (methods) of objects.
A reusable block of code that performs a specific task. Methods can accept parameters and return values.
A keyword (public, private, protected, internal) that controls the visibility and accessibility of a class or its members.
A complete instruction in a program, such as a variable declaration, method call, or control flow directive. Statements end with a semicolon.
A combination of values, variables, operators, and method calls that evaluates to a single value.

data.title: Exercise: Build a Simple Library
data.description: Create a small project that demonstrates understanding of namespaces, classes, and methods.
steps: Create a new console project: `dotnet new console -n SimpleLibrary`
Create a `Book` class inside a `SimpleLibrary.Models` namespace
Add properties: Title, Author, Pages (all strings or ints)
Add a method `AddBook(Book book)` and `ListBooks()` to the Library class
In Program.cs, create a Library instance and add 3 books
data.expectedOutcome: A working console application with properly organized namespaces, classes, and methods that manages a collection of books.

items.question: Do I always need a namespace and class?
items.answer: No. With C# 9.0+ top-level statements, you can write code directly without an explicit class. However, namespaces and classes are still used for organizing larger codebases and are fundamental to C#.

items.question: What's the difference between a class and an object?
items.answer: A class is the blueprint or definition (like an architectural plan). An object (also called an instance) is created from that blueprint (like a house built from the plan). `var book = new Book();` creates an object from the Book class.

items.question: Why do we use namespaces?
items.answer: Namespaces prevent naming conflicts. For example, two different libraries might both have a `Logger` class. Using namespaces like `MyApp.Logging` and `ThirdParty.Logging` keeps them distinct.

items.question: What does 'static' mean?
items.answer: A static member belongs to the class itself rather than to any specific instance. You access it with the class name (e.g., `Math.Max()`) rather than through an object. The Main method is static because the CLR calls it without creating an instance of the Program class.

items.question: Can I have multiple classes in one file?
items.answer: Yes, but the convention in C# is one public class per file, with the filename matching the class name (e.g., `User.cs` contains the `User` class). Non-public classes can share a file if closely related.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Namespaces organize related types and prevent naming conflicts
Classes are blueprints for objects, containing fields, properties, and methods
Access modifiers (public, private, protected, internal) control visibility
Methods define reusable behavior and can return values
Statements perform actions; expressions produce values
One class per file is the standard convention
data.takeaway: Mastering these structural elements is essential for writing well-organized C# applications.
